practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Arguments for: material deprivation, cultural capital, Halsey's research showing class persists even controlling for ability, Ball's research on how marketisation advantages middle-class families. Arguments against or complicating: gender gap — girls now outperform boys regardless of class, suggesting gender is also significant; ethnicity — ethnic group differences cut across class (some working-class ethnic minority pupils outperform middle-class White pupils); interactionist focus on labelling and streaming as in-school processes that may independently shape outcomes regardless of home background. At least two perspectives developed with named sociologists. Sustained sociological vocabulary. Clear judgement weighing whether class is the single most important factor or whether it intersects with gender and ethnicity. Secure (7-9): Both sides covered, named sociologists, judgement present. Developing (4-6): Relevant but one-sided; some named theorists; assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Basic description, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes 'relative poverty'?
A) A condition in which a person lacks enough food to survive physically
B) A condition in which a person earns less than the national average wage
C) A condition in which a person lacks the resources to participate in the standard of living considered normal in their society
D) A condition caused by an individual's unwillingness to seek employment
practice_questions.marks: C) A condition in which a person lacks the resources to participate in the standard of living considered normal in their society [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'absolute poverty'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that absolute poverty refers to a lack of basic necessities; 1 mark for specifying what those necessities are or explaining the fixed nature of the threshold (e.g. 'Absolute poverty is a condition in which an individual lacks the minimum resources required for physical survival, such as adequate food, shelter and clothing, measured against a fixed threshold that does not vary with overall living standards in society.').

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe Townsend's concept of 'relative deprivation'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Townsend defined relative deprivation as lacking resources to participate in the standard of living considered normal in society. 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Townsend (1979) argued that poverty should be measured not just by income but by a deprivation index covering diet, housing, health, education and social activities. Households that could not afford activities considered normal by the majority — such as a birthday meal or taking part in community events — were counted as deprived. Using this approach, Townsend found over 22% of the UK population was living in poverty in 1968–69, far more than government statistics suggested.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Murray's New Right explanation of poverty, including the concept of the underclass.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Murray argued that welfare benefits created a growing underclass dependent on state support rather than employment (1 mark); he identified a dependency culture — a set of values normalising benefit receipt and undermining work and family responsibility (1 mark); he identified rising lone parenthood, crime and youth unemployment as signs of underclass growth in Britain (1 mark); critics argue Murray's evidence is weak, that most benefit recipients hold conventional values and want paid work, and that his analysis ignores structural causes of poverty (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way a Marxist sociologist would explain the existence of poverty in a capitalist society.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Marxists explain poverty as a product of class exploitation inherent to capitalism. 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Marxists argue that poverty results from the fundamental relationship between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat. The bourgeoisie extract surplus value from workers' labour, keeping wages as low as possible to maximise profit. This structural exploitation means working-class people are systematically kept in a position of material deprivation, and globalisation has intensified this by moving manufacturing to lower-wage economies and increasing labour market insecurity.'

practice_questions.text: Sociologists agree that poverty is best explained by the attitudes and behaviour of the poor themselves. How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The cultural explanation (Murray's New Right underclass, dependency culture) is explained in depth as the statement's supporting view. At least two counter-perspectives are developed: Townsend's structural relative deprivation approach (poverty as lack of resources for social participation, measured by deprivation index, finding 22% in poverty); Marxist explanation (poverty as product of class exploitation, structural inequality, bourgeoisie/proletariat relationship); feminist critique of Murray (focuses on lone-parent families, blames women, ignores structural causes of female poverty — gender pay gap, domestic responsibilities). A supported judgement weighs cultural versus structural explanations.

Secure: Both cultural and structural sides present; named sociologists cited; judgement offered.

Developing: Relevant but mostly one perspective; some sociological vocabulary; weak conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description, few named sociologists, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of informal social control?
A) A judge sentencing an offender to a community service order
B) A police officer arresting a suspect under suspicion of theft
C) A parent setting a curfew for their teenage child to be home by 10pm
D) A prison officer supervising inmates during a work period
practice_questions.marks: C) A parent setting a curfew for their teenage child to be home by 10pm [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what sociologists mean by the term 'social control'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying social control as the mechanisms through which societies encourage conformity to norms and discourage deviant behaviour. 1 mark for distinguishing formal and informal forms or for adding that social control operates through both legal authority (formal) and everyday social interaction (informal). Full answer: the mechanisms, formal and informal, by which societies regulate behaviour and encourage conformity to norms and rules.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way in which the family acts as an agency of informal social control.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the family as an informal agency of social control and giving a specific example (e.g. parents setting rules, enforcing curfews, rewarding conformity, sanctioning misbehaviour). 2 marks for a developed description that explains how this mechanism works and its sociological significance: e.g. through primary socialisation, parents embed norms and values about acceptable behaviour before formal institutions are encountered; the positive sanctions (praise, rewards) and negative sanctions (punishment, withdrawal of privileges) teach children the rules of social life. Feminist sociologists note that this control operates differently for boys and girls, with daughters typically facing tighter restrictions.

practice_questions.text: Describe Heidensohn's feminist explanation for women's lower rates of criminal behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying Heidensohn's argument that women face more intensive patriarchal control than men, making it harder to deviate. 1 mark for describing control in the home: domestic expectations, male violence as an assertion of authority, financial dependence on male breadwinners. 1 mark for control in public: threat of male sexual violence, separate spheres ideology limiting independent movement. 1 mark for control at work: male-dominated hierarchies, sexual harassment and limited organisational power. Or: 2 marks for two well-developed domains of control with clear explanation of how each restricts women's opportunities to offend.

practice_questions.text: Sociologists agree that social control is necessary to maintain social order. How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses multiple perspectives with developed arguments and a supported judgement. Arguments in support: functionalist view (Durkheim — social control maintains value consensus, boundary maintenance function of punishment; without control, anomie results and social order breaks down). Arguments qualifying or challenging: Marxist view (social control primarily serves bourgeois interests — policing and imprisonment disproportionately target the working class, while corporate crime is under-controlled; social control is an instrument of class power rather than a neutral mechanism); feminist view (Heidensohn — social control operates intensively on women through patriarchal mechanisms in home, public and work; formal and informal control are both gendered; control does not operate equally across social groups); interactionist view (Becker — social control through labelling can amplify deviance rather than reduce it, through deviancy amplification and the self-fulfilling prophecy; control is not always effective or beneficial). Student names at least two sociologists or perspectives and develops the argument. Reaches a supported judgement that considers the evidence on both sides.

Secure: Both sides covered, named theorists present, judgement reached.

Developing: Relevant arguments but mostly one-sided or undeveloped, some theorists named, conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic descriptions, few named theorists, little evaluative judgement.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one difference between formal and informal social control.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying one clear difference (e.g. formal control uses legal authority and state power; informal control uses social pressure and norms without legal backing). 2 marks for a developed description of both sides of the distinction: formal control is exercised by official agencies (police, courts, prisons) with the power to impose legal penalties such as fines or imprisonment; informal control is exercised by everyday social groups (family, peers, media) through non-legal rewards and sanctions such as approval, ridicule or exclusion. The key distinction is between state-backed legal authority on one hand and social pressure on the other.

practice_questions.text:
Which sampling method involves selecting every tenth person from a list of the population?
A) Random sample
B) Quota sample
C) Systematic sample
D) Snowball sample
practice_questions.marks: C) Systematic sample [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'hypothesis' as used in sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating a hypothesis is a prediction or statement to be tested; 1 mark for indicating it predicts a relationship between variables and can be supported or refuted by evidence. Example: 'A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction about a relationship between two or more variables, stated before data collection and either supported or refuted by the findings.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one advantage of using a pilot study and describe how it would improve the quality of a sociological investigation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an advantage (e.g. identifies flaws in questions, reveals ambiguity, indicates how long the study will take, tests whether the sampling method is practical). Up to 2 marks for a developed description. Example: identifying that a pilot study identifies ambiguous questions (1 mark) and explaining that if a question is unclear to respondents, different participants will interpret it differently, reducing the validity and reliability of the data; revising the question after the pilot ensures all participants understand it in the same way (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between quantitative and qualitative data, and explain why sociologists might choose one over the other.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for describing the difference: quantitative data is numerical (percentages, rates, counts) and allows statistical analysis and large-scale comparison; qualitative data is verbal (words, accounts, meanings) and provides depth and insight into participants' experiences. Up to 2 marks for explaining a reason to choose one. Example: a sociologist studying national patterns of divorce might choose quantitative data (ONS statistics) because it allows trends over time to be identified across the whole population; a sociologist studying the experience of family breakdown for individual children might choose qualitative data (in-depth interviews) because the lived experience requires depth of understanding that statistics cannot provide.

practice_questions.text: Identify one limitation of using official statistics as a source of data in sociological research and describe how this affects the validity of conclusions drawn from them.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a limitation of official statistics (e.g. under-reporting, dark figure of crime, political production, recording inconsistencies between police forces, changing legal definitions). Up to 2 marks for developing the description. Example: identifying under-reporting (1 mark) and explaining that many crimes are never reported to the police — particularly domestic violence and sexual assault — so official crime statistics significantly undercount the true level of offending; any conclusions about crime patterns drawn from official statistics may therefore reflect reporting behaviour rather than actual crime, threatening the validity of the findings (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: "Official statistics are the most useful source of data for sociological research." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments in favour include: official statistics cover the entire population, are free to access, allow long-term trend analysis, and carry the authority of consistent national collection (e.g. ONS, Crime Survey for England and Wales). Arguments against include: official statistics are produced by governments and may reflect political priorities; crime statistics are limited by the dark figure of unreported and unrecorded crime; different sociological perspectives interpret the same statistics differently (functionalist, Marxist and interactionist readings of crime data diverge significantly); qualitative data may offer insight that statistics obscure. The answer cites at least two sociological perspectives or contexts (e.g. crime vs family research), evaluates specific strengths and weaknesses in context, and reaches a clear supported judgement. Sustained sociological vocabulary.

Secure: Both strengths and limitations addressed. At least one sociological perspective cited. A judgement reached.

Developing: Mostly one-sided or descriptive. Some evaluation but undeveloped. Conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic points about what statistics are. Little evaluation. No clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of authority is based on formal rules and offices, where people obey the rules rather than the individual?
A) Traditional authority
B) Charismatic authority
C) Rational-legal authority
D) Informal authority
practice_questions.marks: C) Rational-legal authority [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'authority' as used by sociologists.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that authority involves the exercise of power; 1 mark for specifying that it is considered legitimate — people accept or recognise the right of the person or institution to exercise power over them. Example: 'Authority is the exercise of power that is accepted as legitimate by those over whom it is exercised, meaning people comply because they recognise the right of the authority figure or institution to issue commands.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one of Weber's three types of authority.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly naming one of the three types (traditional, charismatic or rational-legal). 2 marks for a developed description of its source of legitimacy and a relevant example: e.g. 'Traditional authority is based on long-established custom and the inherited status of rulers — people obey because this is how authority has always operated, not because of any formal rule or personal quality. A UK example is the monarchy, where the Crown's legitimacy rests on hereditary succession over centuries rather than electoral mandate or personal charisma.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between formal and informal sources of power, using sociological examples.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Formal power operates through official institutions, laws and constitutional offices — examples include the legal authority of a judge, the constitutional authority of an elected MP, or the formal disciplinary powers of a school head teacher (1 mark, developed 2 marks). Informal power operates outside official structures through social relationships, economic position, cultural influence, norms or peer pressure — examples include an employer's power to dismiss or reward workers, patriarchal informal control within family relationships, or status groups exercising social closure to restrict access to valued positions (1 mark, developed 2 marks). Any two well-developed examples from different categories earn 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe the concept of charismatic authority, including why it is considered unstable.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying charismatic authority as authority based on exceptional personal qualities of a leader. 2 marks for a developed description: 'Charismatic authority derives from followers' belief in the leader's special personal qualities — their vision, magnetism or perceived special destiny. Followers obey because of who the person is, not because of any formal rule or traditional position. It is inherently unstable because it depends on the continued personal devotion of followers and cannot easily be passed on when the leader dies or loses credibility. When charismatic authority collapses it typically either disappears or is routinised into traditional or rational-legal form.'

practice_questions.text: Sociologists agree that power in modern societies is exercised legitimately and in the interests of all. How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of arguments from contrasting perspectives. Supporting the view: functionalist perspective sees rational-legal authority as a functional necessity for social order, benefiting all members of society; Weber's framework acknowledges legitimate authority as genuinely accepted. Against: Marxist perspective argues authority structures serve the interests of the bourgeoisie — ruling class ideology makes class-based power appear neutral and legitimate; formal legal frameworks protect property rights of the wealthy. Feminist perspective: authority structures have been historically patriarchal — traditional and rational-legal authority long excluded women from power; formal equality does not erase structural patriarchy. Named concepts (rational-legal, traditional, charismatic, patriarchy, ruling class ideology, social closure) used throughout. A supported judgement weighs how far power in modern Britain is genuinely legitimate versus how far it reflects class and gender interests.

Secure: Both sides covered; named sociologists/concepts; judgement offered.

Developing: Relevant points, mostly one-sided or underdeveloped; some vocabulary; weak conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description; few named theorists; little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of observation involves the researcher joining the group and participating in their daily life?
A) Structured observation
B) Non-participant observation
C) Participant observation
D) Documentary research
practice_questions.marks: C) Participant observation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'triangulation' as used in sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating it involves using more than one method or data source; 1 mark for indicating the purpose is to cross-check findings or compensate for the weaknesses of individual methods, improving confidence in conclusions. Example: 'Triangulation involves using two or more research methods or sources of data in the same study so that the weaknesses of one approach can be compensated for by the strengths of another, increasing confidence in the validity of the findings.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one advantage of using unstructured interviews and describe why this makes them suitable for studying sensitive social topics.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an advantage of unstructured interviews (e.g. generates rich qualitative data, allows participants to raise unexpected themes, builds rapport, follows the participant's own framework of meaning). Up to 2 marks for describing why this suits sensitive topics. Example: identifying that unstructured interviews build rapport (1 mark) and explaining that for sensitive topics such as domestic abuse or bereavement, the conversational and non-directive format allows participants to feel more comfortable sharing personal experiences; the interviewer can adjust tone and pacing in response to emotional cues, producing more honest and valid data than a standardised questionnaire would (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe the strengths and weaknesses of questionnaires as a method of sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for strengths: questionnaires can reach a large sample quickly and at low cost; responses are standardised so data can be compared statistically; anonymity may increase honest responses on sensitive topics; the study can be replicated, improving reliability. Up to 2 marks for weaknesses: response rates may be low and non-respondents may differ from respondents in ways that bias the findings; closed questions impose the researcher's categories on complex experiences; questionnaires cannot probe or follow up answers; respondents from different social groups may interpret the same question differently, reducing validity.

practice_questions.text: Identify one difference between participant observation and non-participant observation, and describe how this difference affects the quality of data produced.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant difference (e.g. degree of researcher involvement; access to meanings vs detached counting; risk of 'going native' vs risk of Hawthorne effect). Up to 2 marks for developing the description. Example: identifying that participant observation gives the researcher access to the meanings participants attach to their behaviour (1 mark) and explaining that by joining the group, the sociologist can observe behaviour as it naturally occurs and ask participants directly what their actions mean to them — Willis's study of 'the lads' is an example of how participant observation revealed the active resistance and counter-school culture that survey data had not captured (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: "Participant observation is the most valuable method for sociological research." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments in favour: participant observation produces highly valid data that captures real behaviour in natural settings; Willis (1977) reveals depth of counter-school culture not accessible by questionnaire; interactionists value it for accessing meanings. Arguments against: raises serious ethical concerns (deception in covert observation violates informed consent); researcher safety may be compromised studying criminal or dangerous groups; researcher may 'go native' (lose objectivity); extremely time-consuming; findings are not generalisable beyond the specific group; positivist/functionalist researchers argue low reliability (cannot be replicated). The answer evaluates both practical, ethical and theoretical dimensions, cites at least two sociological perspectives or named studies, and reaches a clear supported judgement about when and for whom participant observation is most valuable.

Secure: Arguments for and against addressed. At least one named study or perspective cited. A judgement reached.

Developing: Mostly one-sided or descriptive. Some evaluation but undeveloped. Conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic description of participant observation. Little evaluation. No clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which term describes the process by which a label attached to a pupil causes them to behave in ways that confirm the label?
A) Streaming
B) Cultural deprivation
C) Self-fulfilling prophecy
D) Correspondence principle
practice_questions.marks: C) Self-fulfilling prophecy [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'labelling' in the context of education.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that labelling involves teachers (or others) attaching definitions or categories to pupils; 1 mark for explaining the consequence (that these labels shape how pupils are treated and how they come to see themselves). Example: 'Labelling in education refers to the process by which teachers and others attach definitions — such as "bright", "disruptive" or "low ability" — to pupils. These labels then shape subsequent interactions and the pupil's own self-concept, influencing their behaviour and achievement.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one finding from Ball's 'Beachside Comprehensive' study.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid finding (e.g. banding shaped pupils' trajectories / lower band pupils received a less academic curriculum / teacher expectations differed between bands / working-class pupils were disproportionately placed in lower bands); 2 marks for a developed description explaining the significance. Example: 'Ball found that pupils placed in lower bands at Beachside Comprehensive received a less academic curriculum and had lower expectations placed on them by teachers. The act of banding was not a neutral administrative process — it shaped the educational opportunities available to pupils, and working-class pupils were disproportionately placed in lower bands, reinforcing class inequality.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Willis's concept of 'counter-school culture' as found in his 1977 study 'Learning to Labour'.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks for two developed points. Point 1: Willis followed twelve working-class boys ('the lads') in a West Midlands comprehensive. He found that they developed a counter-school culture that actively rejected the school's values of academic work, obedience and qualifications. They valued masculine toughness, resistance to authority and manual labour, and saw conformist peers ('ear'oles') as passive and weak. Point 2: Paradoxically, this active resistance — which the lads experienced as freedom — prepared them just as effectively for working-class factory jobs as conformity would have done. Willis used this finding to argue that working-class pupils are not passive (contra Bowles and Gintis) but that their agency ultimately reproduces the class structure.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way in which the feminist perspective explains gendered processes within schools.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid gendered process (e.g. gendered teacher expectations / subject channelling / girls expected to be compliant and quiet / boys expected to be more disruptive); 2 marks for a developed description. Example: 'Feminist sociologists argue that teachers hold gendered expectations of pupils: girls may be expected to be quietly diligent and suited to humanities subjects, while boys may be seen as naturally more suited to science and mathematics. These differential expectations shape subject choices and career paths, reproducing occupational gender segregation even after formal barriers to equal access have been removed.'

practice_questions.text: "The processes that take place within schools are the most important cause of educational inequality." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Arguments for: interactionist evidence — labelling theory (Becker on master status), self-fulfilling prophecy, Ball's Beachside Comprehensive (banding and teacher expectations), Willis's counter-school culture showing active in-school processes of class reproduction. Arguments against: Marxists argue in-school processes reflect and reproduce wider class inequality caused by capitalism and material conditions outside school (Bowles and Gintis); feminists note that gender inequality originates in patriarchy beyond schools; Halsey's research shows class affects outcomes even before secondary school banding takes effect. At least two perspectives developed with named sociologists. Sustained sociological vocabulary. Clear judgement weighing in-school processes against out-of-school structural factors. Secure (7-9): Both sides, named sociologists, judgement present. Developing (4-6): Mostly one-sided, some named theorists, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Basic description, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes Zaretsky's Marxist view of the family?
A) The family is a positive institution that performs essential functions for society
B) The family serves capitalism by reproducing the labour force and absorbing worker discontent
C) The family has become more equal as women have entered paid employment
D) The family performs primary socialisation and stabilises adult personalities
practice_questions.marks: B) The family serves capitalism by reproducing the labour force and absorbing worker discontent [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'empty shell marriage'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating that the marriage continues legally; 1 mark for indicating that the emotional relationship between partners has effectively ended. Example: 'An empty shell marriage is one that continues legally but in which the partners have ceased to have a meaningful emotional relationship with each other.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one feminist criticism of the role and status of women within families.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a feminist criticism (e.g. women's domestic labour is exploited; the family is patriarchal; women perform the double shift; the conventional family disguises gender inequality). 2 marks for a developed description naming a feminist sociologist: e.g. 'Delphy and Leonard argued that the family is a patriarchal economic institution in which the husband is the chief beneficiary of all work performed within the household. Women's domestic labour — cooking, child care, emotional management — is appropriated for men's benefit, representing a form of systematic economic exploitation.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the key ideas of Delphy and Leonard on the feminist critique of families.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for naming Delphy and Leonard. 1 mark for identifying their general argument (the family is a patriarchal economic institution). 1 mark for describing the mechanism of exploitation: women's domestic labour (cooking, cleaning, child care, emotional support) is performed for the benefit of the husband/male partner. 1 mark for a developed point: e.g. Delphy and Leonard argued this is not about individual men's attitudes but a structural arrangement in which men as a class systematically benefit from women's unpaid work, making the family an institution of gender inequality rather than mutual support.

practice_questions.text: Describe the criticism that the nuclear family has become socially isolated.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying isolation as a criticism (the nuclear family has lost contact with wider kinship and community networks). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'As the nuclear family became more privatised and home-centred (following the principle of stratified diffusion described by Willmott and Young), it lost the external support of extended kinship networks. This places intense pressure on individual family members — particularly during crises — and critics argue that isolated families are more vulnerable to conflict, domestic abuse and mental health problems, rather than automatically providing the "warm bath" of emotional support that Parsons described.'

practice_questions.text: "The family is a harmful institution for women." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A sustained two-sided argument. Arguments in support: Feminist view — Oakley argued the conventional family is based on women's unpaid domestic labour; Delphy and Leonard argued the family is a patriarchal economic institution exploiting women; the double shift adds domestic labour to women's paid work; women are more likely to be victims of domestic violence in family settings. Arguments against: Functionalist view — Murdock argued the family performs essential positive functions for all members; Parsons's warm bath theory suggests the family supports both partners. Willmott and Young's march of progress suggests the family has become more equal over time. New Right perspective argues family diversity — not the traditional family — is the source of social problems. At least two named sociologists developed in detail. Sociological vocabulary used accurately (patriarchy, domestic division of labour, double shift, exploitation, primary socialisation). Supported conclusion.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides present, named sociologists referenced, judgement present.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant points, mainly one-sided or undeveloped.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points, mainly description, little judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which piece of legislation in 1969 made divorce substantially easier to obtain in England and Wales by introducing 'irretrievable breakdown of marriage' as grounds for divorce?
A) The Family Law Act 1965
B) The Divorce Reform Act 1969
C) The Marriage Act 1970
D) The Matrimonial Causes Act 1950
practice_questions.marks: B) The Divorce Reform Act 1969 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'secularisation'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a long-term process or trend; 1 mark for explaining that it involves the decline of the social, cultural or institutional influence of religion in society. Example: 'Secularisation is the long-term decline in the social and cultural influence of religion in a society, including reduced church attendance and a weakening of religious authority over personal decisions such as marriage and divorce.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one consequence of divorce for children.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a consequence (e.g. lower educational achievement; poorer health outcomes; disruption of routine and living arrangements; reduced family income). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Sociological research suggests that children whose parents divorce are more likely to experience lower educational achievement and poorer health outcomes compared to children from intact two-parent households. However, sociologists caution that parental conflict — not divorce itself — may be the key factor; children in highly conflicted intact families may be worse off than those in cooperative post-divorce families. Outcomes also vary significantly with income and parenting arrangements.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the reasons why the changing status of women contributed to rising divorce rates in Britain after 1945.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying women's growing participation in paid employment and economic independence. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism: greater economic independence reduced the financial dependence on a male partner that had previously made divorce unviable for many women. 1 mark for a further point: research shows the majority of divorce petitions in Britain are filed by women, supporting the argument that women's changing status enabled more of them to leave unsatisfactory marriages. 1 mark for a developed explanation or link to Oakley: women's rising expectations of marriage — combined with the continuing burden of the double shift — made women less willing to endure unequal or unhappy marriages.

practice_questions.text: Describe the New Right view of rising divorce rates and their consequences.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying the New Right as concerned about rising divorce rates. 1 mark for naming Murray or referencing the New Right's argument that rising divorce contributes to lone parent families. 1 mark for describing the mechanism: lone parent households are argued by the New Right to contribute to a dependency culture and the development of an underclass, associated with poverty, crime and educational underachievement. 1 mark for a developed or critical point: e.g. the New Right views children raised without two parents as educationally and socially disadvantaged. Feminist sociologists challenge this view, arguing it pathologises lone parent families without recognising that poverty and lack of affordable child care — not lone parenthood itself — cause the disadvantages.

practice_questions.text: "Rising divorce rates show that the family as an institution is in decline." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A sustained two-sided argument. Arguments in support (decline): New Right perspective — Murray argued rising divorce and lone parenthood contribute to an underclass and social problems; high divorce rates suggest marriages are failing; children are disadvantaged by family breakdown. Arguments against (not decline): Functionalist view — Parsons argued the family adapts to meet social needs; high remarriage rates show marriage as an institution is still valued (serial monogamy); the Divorce Reform Act 1969 made legal divorce easier, so rates reflect legal change as much as relationship breakdown. Feminist view — rising rates reflect women's growing independence and capacity to leave unhappy marriages; this is progress, not decline. Marxist view — marital breakdown is driven by economic pressures of capitalism, not family values. Empty shell marriage as evidence that official divorce statistics undercount breakdown. At least two named sociologists developed in detail. Sociological vocabulary (serial monogamy, empty shell marriage, secularisation, Divorce Reform Act, underclass, lone parent family) used accurately. Supported conclusion.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides present, named sociologists, judgement present.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant points, mainly one-sided or undeveloped.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points, mainly description, little judgement.

practice_questions.text:
According to Walby, how many structures of patriarchy operate to restrict women's power?
A) Three
B) Four
C) Five
D) Six
practice_questions.marks: D) Six [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'patriarchy' as used by feminist sociologists.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that patriarchy refers to a system in which men hold power; 1 mark for clarifying that it is a structural or systemic concept in which women are systematically disadvantaged across social institutions (not just that individual men dominate individual women). Example: 'Patriarchy is a structural system in which men hold dominant positions of power across social institutions — employment, the family, the state — and women are systematically disadvantaged as a result.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe two of Walby's six structures of patriarchy.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per structure. For each: 1 mark for correctly naming and briefly identifying the structure; 1 mark for a developed description with a sociological example. Paid work: women face the glass ceiling, the gender pay gap and concentration in lower-paid 'feminised' occupations despite formal equality legislation. Household production: women carry a disproportionate share of unpaid domestic labour even when in full-time employment — the double shift. Patriarchal culture: double standards operate on women's behaviour in areas such as sexual conduct and public appearance. Sexuality: women face double standards on sexual behaviour — behaviour admired in men is judged negatively in women. Male violence: the use or threat of violence constrains women's behaviour in public and reinforces patriarchal authority. The state: women remain under-represented in elected and appointed positions; equal pay laws are weakly enforced.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe the difference between private patriarchy and public patriarchy as described by Walby.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Walby distinguished two forms of patriarchy. 2 marks for a developed description: 'Private patriarchy involves direct personal control of women by individual men — fathers or husbands — largely confining women to the private domestic sphere with minimal access to public life, employment or legal rights. Public patriarchy characterises contemporary Western society: women have formal access to public life but are collectively disadvantaged within it — segregated into lower-paid occupations, under-represented in leadership, and subject to a gender pay gap. Walby argues that while the form has changed, patriarchy continues to maintain male dominance.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way that age affects power relationships in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying one way (e.g. ageism in the labour market; older people's under-representation in political power; young people excluded from key financial and political decisions). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Older workers in the UK face ageism in the labour market — discriminatory attitudes and practices that lead to their being passed over for promotion or made redundant before younger colleagues. This limits their economic power and income security. Older people may also have reduced political representation as elected bodies have historically been dominated by middle-aged adults, and their interests in areas such as social care funding may be under-prioritised.'

practice_questions.text: Sociologists agree that gender remains the most important factor shaping unequal power relationships in modern society. How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Walby's feminist analysis is presented in depth — six structures of patriarchy, private versus public patriarchy, gender pay gap, glass ceiling as evidence. At least one contrasting perspective is developed: functionalist view (gender roles as functional specialisation reflecting expressive and instrumental division); Marxist view (power relationships fundamentally rooted in class conflict; gender inequality serves capitalism). Other dimensions of power relationships — class, ethnicity, age, disability — are acknowledged as potentially equally or additionally important, introducing the concept of intersectionality. A supported judgement is made about whether gender is the most important single factor or whether multiple intersecting dimensions offer a more complete account.

Secure: Both sides present, named sociologists cited, judgement offered.

Developing: Relevant but mostly one perspective; some vocabulary; weak conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description; few named theorists; little evaluation.

before.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Describe question on Walby’s six structures of patriarchy, do not simply list all six without explanation — this scores in the lower band. The mark scheme rewards depth: name two or three structures, describe each one clearly and link them to examples (the glass ceiling and gender pay gap for paid work; the double shift for household production; male violence and Heidensohn’s work on female conformity for the violence structure). On a 12-mark Discuss about patriarchy or gender inequality, always contrast Walby’s feminist analysis with the functionalist view (gender roles as functional specialisation) and/or the Marxist view (inequality rooted in class conflict). Close with a judgement about whether patriarchy or class conflict better explains gender inequality in contemporary Britain.

practice_questions.text:
Which research method did Willis use in his 1977 study 'Learning to Labour'?
A) Structured questionnaire
B) Analysis of official statistics
C) Participant observation
D) Non-participant observation
practice_questions.marks: C) Participant observation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'informed consent' as it applies to sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that informed consent means participants agree to take part in research; 1 mark for specifying that they must be told what the research involves and have the right to withdraw. Example: 'Informed consent means that participants agree to take part in a research study after being told clearly what it involves, why it is being conducted, and that they have the right to withdraw at any time without penalty.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one practical problem sociologists face when conducting research in schools.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid practical issue (access through gatekeepers / time and cost of qualitative research / researcher influence changing classroom dynamics / obtaining parental consent); 2 marks for a developed description. Example: 'Gaining access to schools requires the permission of several gatekeepers — the headteacher must agree to the research, individual class teachers must allow the researcher into their classrooms, and parents must give consent for their children to participate. Each level of gatekeeping can limit what the researcher can access: headteachers may only allow observation of their best lessons, meaning the data does not represent everyday school life and lacks validity.'

practice_questions.text: Describe one strength and one weakness of using official statistics (such as GCSE results data) to research educational achievement.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks for two developed points. Strength: official statistics from the Department for Education are large-scale, covering all schools in England, and longitudinal — allowing researchers to track trends in achievement by class, gender and ethnicity over many years. This gives high reliability: the same data can be checked and compared by other researchers. Weakness: official statistics are socially constructed — they reflect decisions about what to measure. League table positions measure exam results but not the value added to pupils' progress. A school with a disadvantaged intake scoring below the national average may be more effective than a school in a wealthy area scoring higher, but the statistics do not capture this.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one ethical issue that arises when interviewing pupils about their experience of labelling by teachers.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid ethical issue (harm to participants / confidentiality / informed consent with minors); 2 marks for a developed description applying the issue to this specific context. Example: 'Harm to participants is a key ethical issue when asking pupils to discuss their experience of being labelled by teachers. This may involve recounting humiliating or upsetting experiences — being placed in the bottom set, being told they are unlikely to pass their GCSEs — which could cause psychological distress. Researchers address this by using sensitive interview techniques, ensuring pupils know they can stop at any time, and providing a debriefing session at the end. However, there is a tension: the more honestly pupils speak, the more useful the data, but also the greater the potential for distress.'

practice_questions.text: "Participant observation is the best method for sociologists researching what happens inside schools." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Arguments for: participant observation generates high validity — the researcher accesses participants' genuine perspectives and behaviours in natural settings; Willis's Learning to Labour is the classic example, revealing counter-school culture that a questionnaire could not have captured. Arguments against: practical problems — access requires multiple gatekeepers; researcher presence changes classroom dynamics (reducing validity through the Hawthorne effect); time-consuming and expensive; findings may not be generalisable (Willis studied twelve boys in one school). Alternative methods: official statistics allow large-scale analysis of achievement trends (Halsey's Origins and Destinations); interviews allow targeted exploration of specific issues; mixed methods (triangulation) allow checks on reliability and validity. At least two methods evaluated with reference to named studies or sociologists. Sustained sociological vocabulary. Clear judgement about whether participant observation is 'best' in context or whether it depends on the research question. Secure (7-9): Both sides evaluated, named examples, judgement present. Developing (4-6): Mostly one-sided, some named examples, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Basic description of one method, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which term describes individuals or organisations who control access to a research population and whose permission must be obtained before research begins?
A) Respondents
B) Gatekeepers
C) Sampling frames
D) Pilot participants
practice_questions.marks: B) Gatekeepers [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'informed consent' as used in sociological research ethics.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating consent requires participants to agree to take part; 1 mark for indicating they must be given full, honest information about the study and must agree voluntarily, with the right to withdraw. Example: 'Informed consent means that research participants must be given clear and honest information about the study, including its purpose and how their data will be used, and must voluntarily agree to take part before data collection begins.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one practical issue that sociologists face when conducting research and describe how it can affect the quality of the data collected.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a practical issue (time, cost or access). Up to 2 marks for describing how it affects data quality. Example: identifying access (1 mark) and describing that if a gatekeeper (such as a school head teacher) restricts access to certain participants — for example, excluding students with poor behaviour records from a study of school exclusion — the resulting sample will be biased and unrepresentative, meaning the findings cannot be generalised and the validity of the research is undermined (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two ethical issues that a sociologist might face when conducting research with vulnerable participants, and explain how each can be addressed.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for the first ethical issue: e.g. harm to participants — discussing traumatic experiences (abuse, bereavement) may cause psychological distress; the researcher can address this by offering a debrief session after the interview, providing signposting to relevant support services, and having a clear protocol for stopping if the participant shows signs of distress (1 mark for identifying harm, 1 mark for an appropriate solution). Up to 2 marks for the second ethical issue: e.g. informed consent with children — children under 16 usually cannot give consent on their own; the researcher must obtain written consent from a parent or guardian as well as assent from the child, and must explain the research in age-appropriate language (1 mark for identifying the consent problem, 1 mark for the practical solution).

practice_questions.text: Identify one ethical problem created by using covert observation as a research method and describe how a researcher might attempt to address it.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an ethical problem specific to covert observation (e.g. deception violates informed consent; participants cannot withdraw because they do not know they are being studied; the researcher may observe illegal activity and face a legal or moral dilemma). Up to 2 marks for describing how it might be addressed. Example: identifying that covert observation involves deception, violating informed consent (1 mark) and explaining that some researchers address this by conducting a debrief as soon as the covert phase is complete — informing participants of the research, offering them the right to withdraw their data, and seeking retrospective consent — though critics argue this does not fully resolve the original deception (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: "Ethical guidelines make some of the most valuable sociological research impossible to conduct." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments in favour: some research questions (studying gang violence, covert institutional racism, hidden drug networks) genuinely cannot be investigated ethically through fully consented, transparent methods; the Hawthorne effect means fully transparent research produces less valid data on sensitive behaviour; historical sociological research that violated consent (covert observation of private behaviour) produced findings that shaped policy. Arguments against: ethical guidelines protect vulnerable participants from exploitation; the BSA guidelines provide practical solutions (anonymisation, debriefs, ethics committees) that allow sensitive research to proceed; research that violates ethical principles is rejected by academic journals and ethics committees, and the findings lack credibility; feminist researchers argue participant-centred approaches produce richer and more valid data than covert extraction. At least two perspectives and named methods/examples cited. A clear supported judgement about where the balance lies.

Secure: Both sides addressed. At least one named method or context. A judgement reached.

Developing: Mostly one-sided or descriptive. Some relevant points. Conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic description of ethical issues. Little evaluative engagement. No clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which research method did Ann Oakley use in her study of housework, generating rich qualitative data about women's experiences of domestic labour?
A) Postal questionnaire
B) Official statistics analysis
C) Non-participant observation
D) Unstructured interviews
practice_questions.marks: D) Unstructured interviews [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'informed consent' as used in sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating that participants are given information about the research; 1 mark for indicating that they make a free and voluntary decision to take part. Example: 'Informed consent means that research participants are given sufficient information about the study — its purpose, methods and how data will be used — to make a free and voluntary decision about whether to take part.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one ethical issue that arises specifically when researching families with children.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an ethical issue (e.g. informed consent with children; confidentiality limits when abuse is discovered; risk of harm to child participants). 2 marks for a developed description including how the issue can be addressed: e.g. 'Children below the age of consent cannot legally give consent themselves, so parents or guardians must consent on their behalf. However, sociologists debate whether parental consent alone is sufficient — children may feel unable to refuse if their parents have agreed. One way to address this is to speak to children separately from their parents, making clear that their participation is voluntary and will not affect their relationship with their parents.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the strengths and weaknesses of using official statistics to study divorce and family change in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for a strength: official statistics are nationally representative and produced annually by the ONS, making them a reliable source for identifying broad trends over time (e.g. rising divorce rates after the 1969 Act). 1 mark for a second strength or detail: they are freely available, cover the entire population (unlike small-scale studies) and are consistent across time, allowing longitudinal comparisons. 1 mark for a weakness: official divorce statistics only count legal divorces and miss informal separations (cohabiting couples who split without legal proceedings) and empty shell marriages — meaning they undercount actual relationship breakdown. 1 mark for a second weakness: divorce statistics partly reflect changes in the law (the Divorce Reform Act 1969 caused an immediate spike in figures) rather than changes in relationship quality or behaviour.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one practical challenge a sociologist would face when using observation to study family life.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a practical challenge (e.g. gaining access to private family homes; the Hawthorne effect; changing family composition; time and cost). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'A major practical challenge is gaining access — families are private institutions and most people would be reluctant to allow a researcher to observe their home life. Even when access is granted, families are likely to behave differently when aware of being observed (the Hawthorne effect), which reduces the validity of the data — the researcher may observe an idealised version of family life rather than everyday behaviour.'

practice_questions.text: "Questionnaires are the best method for sociologists studying family life." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A sustained two-sided argument evaluating questionnaires in the specific context of family research. Arguments in support: Willmott and Young used large-scale surveys successfully to identify patterns in the domestic division of labour — questionnaires are practical, cheap to administer to large samples, produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and allows broad trends to be identified. They can be completed anonymously, reducing embarrassment on sensitive topics. Arguments against: questionnaires risk socially desirable responses — Oakley found that Willmott and Young's survey data overstated male domestic participation because respondents gave the 'right' answer rather than an honest one; questionnaires produce limited depth on complex relationships and emotions; closed questions cannot capture the nuances of family experience. Unstructured interviews (Oakley) generate richer data. Observation could provide more naturalistic data but raises access and ethical problems. Mixed methods offer a solution — combining surveys for breadth with interviews for depth. Named sociologists (Willmott and Young, Oakley) developed in detail. Sociological vocabulary used accurately (quantitative, qualitative, validity, reliability, Hawthorne effect, socially desirable response, informed consent). Supported conclusion.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides of the questionnaire debate present, named sociologists, judgement present.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant points, mainly one-sided or undeveloped.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points, mainly description, little judgement.

practice_questions.text:
What term describes the gap between the amount of crime actually committed and the amount recorded in official statistics?
A) The crime rate
B) The dark figure
C) The reliability gap
D) The deviance index
practice_questions.marks: B) The dark figure [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'official crime statistics'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that official crime statistics are government-collected figures on crime; 1 mark for specifying that they are based on crimes reported to and recorded by the police (not all crimes committed). Example: 'Official crime statistics are government-produced data on crime, based on crimes recorded by the police. They are a form of secondary data and are published annually, but they do not include crimes that are unreported or unrecorded.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one practical challenge of researching crime using participant observation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a specific practical challenge (e.g. gaining access to criminal or deviant groups; researcher safety; covert versus overt dilemma; small, unrepresentative samples). 2 marks for a developed description in context: e.g. 'Gaining access to active offenders or gang members is a major practical challenge. Potential participants may distrust researchers, fear criminal exposure, or be difficult to locate through conventional sampling methods. Sociologists often use snowball sampling — using initial contacts to recruit further participants — but this produces a sample that is unlikely to be representative of all offenders. Willis's use of participant observation in a school was more straightforward than studying active criminal subcultures, where safety concerns and legal issues create additional obstacles.'

practice_questions.text: Describe one strength and one weakness of using self-report studies to research crime.
practice_questions.marks: Strength (up to 2 marks): Self-report studies capture offending that never comes to official attention, giving a broader picture of crime patterns than police-recorded statistics. They have consistently shown that offending is more evenly distributed across social classes than official statistics suggest, challenging the view that crime is primarily a working-class problem and supporting the interactionist critique that official statistics reflect selective enforcement rather than true offending patterns (2 marks). Weakness (up to 2 marks): Respondents may under-report serious or embarrassing offences even when anonymity is guaranteed, reducing validity. Samples are also typically drawn from accessible populations such as school students, missing offenders who have dropped out of education or the most serious, prolific offenders (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one ethical challenge of researching poverty and disadvantaged groups.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an ethical challenge (e.g. harm to participants if identified; exploitation of vulnerable research participants; informed consent with participants who may feel unable to refuse powerful researchers; confidentiality of sensitive financial information). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Researching people living in poverty risks exploiting vulnerable participants who may feel unable to refuse to cooperate with an authoritative researcher. Ensuring genuinely informed consent requires care — participants must understand the purpose of the research and their right to withdraw without consequences. If a study involves revealing personal financial circumstances or experiences of homelessness or domestic violence, strong anonymisation procedures are essential to protect participants from harm. Townsend addressed this partly through questionnaires that were less intrusive than face-to-face interviews, but even anonymous questionnaire data can carry risks if it can be traced back to individuals.'

practice_questions.text: Sociologists agree that official crime statistics are a reliable and valid source of data on crime in England and Wales. How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments. Supporting the view: official statistics provide a long-term, consistent and regularly updated data source enabling trend analysis over many decades; they are the most comprehensive available coverage of police-recorded crime; functionalists might argue they reflect genuine patterns. Against: dark figure — many crimes are unreported (domestic violence, sexual assault, corporate crime); interactionist critique (Becker) — official statistics reflect labelling and police discretion, not true offending rates; Marxist critique — statistics focus on working-class street crime and under-represent corporate and white-collar crime. Comparison with the Crime Survey for England and Wales (which shows higher crime levels) and self-report studies (showing more distributed offending). A supported judgement on whether official statistics are more useful for understanding trends or for measuring the actual level of crime.

Secure: Both sides present with named sociologists/concepts; judgement offered.

Developing: Relevant but mostly one perspective; some contextualised points; weak conclusion.

Emerging: Basic points; generic methods evaluation; little named sociological theory; minimal evaluation.

before.exam_tip_html: The most common error on methods questions is evaluating a method generically rather than in context. If a question asks you to evaluate the use of official statistics to study crime, the mark scheme rewards points specific to crime research: the dark figure, the problem of unreported crimes, police recording decisions, the ideological critique (focusing on working-class street crime). If asked about studying poverty, the mark scheme looks for reference to Townsend’s deprivation index, the debate between validity and reliability, the difficulty of sampling the most deprived households. On a 12-mark Discuss asking how far official statistics are a useful source of data on crime, present the functionalist view (official statistics reflect real patterns of offending and are reliable over time), the interactionist critique (they reflect labelling and police discretion, not true offending patterns) and the Marxist critique (they focus on working-class crime, under-representing corporate and white-collar offending). Close with a supported judgement.
